candidateRows: Agnosticism is the warranted position because God's nonexistence cannot be established, while the observed world still gives reason to doubt a traditional creator.
This establishes the skeptical side's governing position on God's existence and explains why uncertainty nevertheless leans away from traditional creator theism.
Asked to state his current position and intellectual path, O'Connor distinguishes agnosticism from categorical atheism and locates himself on the skeptical side of the question.
The New Atheist claim that religion is simply evil is too reductive, even though religion's possible social value does not make its truth claims credible.
The distinction prevents the skeptical case from resting on religion's social harms and separates the pragmatic value of religion from whether it is true.
O'Connor characterizes New Atheism as combining disbelief with hostility toward religion, then rejects the second component as simplistic while retaining disbelief.
Collins's movement from atheism through uncertainty to Christianity resulted from sustained inquiry and remains a rational commitment despite questions and doubts.
The account frames Christian belief as the considered conclusion of a scientifically trained former atheist rather than inherited certainty or resistance to inquiry.
Collins describes belief as a spectrum, recounts beginning without religion, adopting atheism, and later becoming a Christian whose commitment centers increasingly on Jesus.
God provides evidence sufficient for a free personal commitment rather than coercive mathematical proof that would make belief unavoidable.
This supplies the pro side's epistemic standard, explaining why the absence of demonstrative certainty does not undermine the rationality of Christian belief.
After being asked about proof and evidence, Collins argues that conclusive demonstration would defeat the personal and freely chosen character intended for faith.
The universe's beginning and fine-tuning, objective moral experience, beauty, and the failure of strict atheism jointly make trust in God reasonable.
This is the pro side's cumulative positive case, assembling cosmological, fine-tuning, moral, and aesthetic considerations into a direct rationale for theism.
Collins surveys several converging considerations, contrasts intelligence with a faith-demanding multiverse response, and explains why their accumulation led him to trust God.
Agnosticism is appropriate because the word God lacks a sufficiently comprehensible referent, especially under classical accounts that treat divine attributes as merely analogical.
The argument challenges whether evidence for God can even be assessed before the disputed entity is coherently specified, supporting skepticism at a foundational level.
Collins's claim that multiple observable considerations can count as evidence supporting belief in God.
O'Connor moves from ordinary ambiguity in the term God to classical theological descriptions, arguing that an incomprehensible referent makes evidential judgments deeply uncertain.
Christianity lacks adequate support and conflicts with the same moral intuitions invoked for God, particularly through resurrection evidence and morally troubling biblical material.
This directly contests the specifically Christian conclusion of the motion by challenging both its central historical claim and the moral credibility of its scriptures.
Collins's cumulative case that moral experience and the person of Jesus support movement from general theism to Christianity.
O'Connor distinguishes uncertainty about an undefined deity from skepticism toward Christianity, citing the resurrection and biblical treatments of slavery and women as obstacles.
Life-permitting physical constants require explanation, and an intelligent creator is more plausible than an empirically inaccessible multiverse while also addressing why anything exists.
The argument develops fine-tuning into a principal affirmative inference to divine intelligence and supplements it with the deeper need for an uncaused cause.
Collins explains constants through gravity and cosmic development, argues that small changes prevent complexity, and compares creator theism favorably with multiverse speculation.
Fine-tuning may undermine creator theism because an unconstrained God should not need life to depend on a narrow physical knife edge or hostile meta-conditions.
This is a direct reversal of the pro side's principal scientific argument, contending that apparent fine-tuning is surprising on an omnipotent creator hypothesis.
Collins's argument that precisely life-permitting constants cry out for intelligence and favor a creator over alternative explanations.
O'Connor questions divine constraint, proposes that delicate material conditions fit rival theological stories, and argues that the underlying improbability can count against the intended creator.
Fine-tuning need not identify a uniquely possible universe; God could select an interesting, complex universe from multiple viable configurations.
This qualifies the fine-tuning case by denying that only one precise configuration could realize God's creative purpose.
O'Connor's claim that the narrow life-permitting range reflects badly on a creator who wants a material universe.

After O'Connor argues that overwhelmingly inhospitable possibilities undermine the creator hypothesis, Collins answers that related constants permit multiple solutions and compares creation to an artist selecting a masterpiece.
If God cannot produce the same interesting universe under different physical constants, those constants appear to constrain divine creative power.
The move attacks the fine-tuning inference by asking why an omnipotent creator must work within the life-permitting physical parameters.
Collins's claim that God chose constants yielding an interesting universe rather than a sterile or prematurely collapsing one.
Following Collins's big-crunch explanation, O'Connor distinguishes creating a boring universe from creating the same complex universe through different parameters and asks whether gravity limits God.
God creates through orderly laws, and God's desire for loving relationships guides the selection of physical parameters capable of producing complex creatures.
It supplies the theological premise connecting lawful fine-tuning to God's purposes and explains why alternative constants would not achieve the same end.
O'Connor's objection that differing constants should not prevent an omnipotent God from creating the same complex outcome.
Collins responds that God is a God of order and love who chooses lawful means suited to relationship-capable creatures; with the existing laws, changing gravity alone would defeat that goal.
Physical constants are unlike logical necessities, so treating them as constraints on God creates a genuine challenge to divine omnipotence.
This sharpens the dispute from scientific feasibility to omnipotence and contests the proposed analogy between constants and logical laws.
Collins's assertion that even God could not obtain the same complexity after changing gravity while retaining the other laws.
O'Connor grants that God cannot make contradictions such as two plus two equaling five, but argues that a life-permitting universe with stronger gravity is physically, not logically, contradictory.
Given God's commitments to natural order and relationship with complex creatures, the observed gravity constant is the necessary means to God's chosen ends.
The response concedes a goal-relative constraint while preserving the fine-tuning argument through God's freely adopted purposes and lawful method.
O'Connor's distinction between genuine logical impossibilities and apparently contingent physical limits on divine power.

Collins says equations governing matter and energy need not have existed, but once divine order and relationship-capable life are given, the observed gravity value becomes the means required for those goals.
The immense and apparently unnecessary suffering produced by evolution is expected under atheistic naturalism but surprising under a loving creator hypothesis.
It presents the principal evidential problem of animal suffering against Christian theism and argues that standard human-centered theodicies do not address it.

O'Connor acknowledges fine-tuning's force, then compares worldview predictions: evolutionary history contains vast animal pain, extinction, and predation that naturalism predicts but a loving relational creator seemingly does not.
Evolution's suffering is compatible with a God of order because an elegant lawful creative process can be providentially directed without repeated supernatural interventions.
This is the main theistic answer to the animal-suffering objection, grounding evolutionary costs in stable laws and a creation plan directed toward humanity.
O'Connor's argument that extensive evolutionary animal suffering is far more expected under atheistic naturalism than under loving theism.

Collins grants a hard problem but stresses nature's beauty and animal joy, doubts animals share human mortality anxiety, and argues that evolution lawfully realizes a plan established from the beginning.
Appealing to unknown reasons for suffering permits an equivalent appeal to unknown natural explanations for fine-tuning, while simple alternatives show animal agony was avoidable.
The move rebuts Collins's appeal to ordered evolution both epistemically and substantively, arguing that omnipotence could reduce suffering without abandoning a lawful ecosystem.
Collins's defense that a providential God of order used an elegant evolutionary process governed by stable laws despite its suffering.

O'Connor argues that mystery must cut both ways, proposes herbivorous ecosystems as an obvious improvement, describes predation's severity, and denies that such suffering was necessary for conscious agents able to love God.
Physical suffering follows from stable natural laws, and avoiding it would require continual divine intervention that would compromise God's ordered creation.
It directly answers the claim that animal suffering was avoidable by presenting suffering as an unavoidable package of lawful creation judged worth humanity's advent.
O'Connor's contention that an omnipotent God could preserve an ecosystem and conscious life while eliminating vast predatory suffering.

Collins invokes physical evil such as earthquake deaths as consequences of lawful nature, argues that prevention would demand repeated intervention, and says God judged relationship-capable persons worth the cost.
Historical testimony, the empty tomb, resurrection appearances, and witnesses' costly persistence make Jesus's bodily resurrection the most likely explanation.
The argument directly supports Christian rather than generic theism by defending the central historical miracle and explaining its exceptional suspension of natural law.

Collins first defends Jesus's historical existence and crucifixion, then cites the empty tomb, appearances, witnesses who would not recant, historical scholarship, and God's authority to suspend natural laws exceptionally.
The Gospel accounts warrant suspicion because they combine biography, legend, and theology rather than functioning as uniformly reliable historical reports.
This establishes O'Connor's foundational reason for resisting the resurrection evidence offered for Christian theism.
Collins's claim that the historical evidence makes Jesus's resurrection the most likely explanation.
After Collins defends divine suspension of natural laws and asks for O'Connor's view, O'Connor challenges the historical reliability of the relevant narratives.
Independent attestation across Gospel sources raises historical confidence, whereas a story confined to one source deserves substantially less confidence.
The proposed source-critical method supplies the evidential standard behind O'Connor's skepticism about particular resurrection narratives.
The request for the evidential sources and method used to distinguish reliable from unreliable Gospel material.
O'Connor distinguishes shared and source-specific traditions, using crucifixion and doubting Thomas to illustrate differing levels of historical confidence.
The theological purposes and genres of Gospel texts help explain why singly attested divine claims are less historically secure than multiply attested material.
This extends the source-critical case by connecting Johannine theology to reduced confidence in unique claims about Jesus's divinity.
Collins's contention that a unique story need not be doubted merely because it appears in only one Gospel.
O'Connor clarifies comparative confidence, analyzes John's theological purpose, and contrasts broadly attested traditions with a unique explicit divinity claim.
The resurrection appearances are better explained as later mythological development because earlier Mark lacks them and later sources become more elaborate.
This is a direct alternative explanation of the central resurrection evidence offered to make Christian theism more plausible.
Collins's request for O'Connor's account of what occurred after the historically accepted crucifixion of Jesus.
O'Connor compares the earliest form of Mark with later Gospels and argues that increasing detail and theology fit legendary growth.
Claims that the disciples died for resurrection belief are historically uncertain, while Paul's earlier testimony is not bodily eyewitness testimony and permits ordinary mistake.
The move challenges two principal supports for the resurrection case: martyrdom sincerity and the early testimony attributed to Paul.
Collins's appeal to the disciples' deaths and Paul's early creed as corroboration of the resurrection.
O'Connor questions the historical foundation of disciple martyrdom and argues that Paul's visionary experience is less probative than physical interaction.
Cross-cultural recognition of good and evil points beyond evolutionary explanation toward a holy source of goodness and love.
The argument directly advances morality as evidence that a personal and loving God is more plausible than a purely naturalistic account.
O'Connor's argument that morally objectionable biblical practices undermine a Judeo-Christian claim to moral insight.
Collins distinguishes disagreement about which acts are good from widespread belief that good and evil exist, then infers a transcendent moral source.
The New Testament's sweeping portrayal of Jesus and its resurrection case can rationally compel commitment without resolving every textual dispute or attaining proof.
This supplies Collins's holistic defense of Christian revelation and resurrection despite acknowledged uncertainty in detailed historical scholarship.
O'Connor's source-critical objections concerning Gospel development, disputed traditions, and the historical resurrection case.
Collins acknowledges limited engagement with source debates but argues that Jesus's radical teaching and the cumulative resurrection case remain compelling.
A surprising and unwanted message received in prayer can function as personal revelation that supplements rational argument and supports religious commitment.
The personal-revelation account directly advances revelation as an additional path from rational proximity to committed Christian belief.
The question whether belief or nonbelief must follow a wholly rational path or may legitimately include revelation.
Collins recounts a specific prayer experience, explains why he did not regard the message as self-generated, and connects revelation to his conversion.
Personal revelation could legitimately raise one's belief in God, but private experience has little force as public evidence and intellectual argument cannot be the only accessible route.
The move defines O'Connor's qualified openness to revelation while limiting its interpersonal evidential force and rejecting an elitist path to faith.
Collins's account of receiving an unexpected prayer message and his question about what revelation could change O'Connor's mind.
O'Connor says a sufficiently theological experience could affect his credence, distinguishes personal warrant from debate evidence, and emphasizes accessibility.
Experiences of numinous beauty and musical longing can provide fleeting indications of a transcendent reality that ordinary natural description may miss.
The move directly introduces beauty and numinous longing as experiential considerations favoring theism within the stated motion.
After discussion of revelation and divine accessibility, Collins turns to beauty, describing music-induced longing as a possible glimpse of something more.
The diversity of things called beautiful makes it difficult to infer a single intrinsic maximum of beauty resembling God.
It directly challenges whether aesthetic longing supplies a coherent argument from beauty to God, one of the motion's specified grounds.
The earlier suggestion that experiences of beauty and longing may point toward God or transcendent reality.
After distinguishing several categorically different uses of beauty, O'Connor questions what longing seeks and doubts that varied aesthetic attractions combine into a God-like object.
Beauty often feels like an ache tied to suffering and perceived disconnection between the world and how it ought to be.
The move offers a substantive alternative account of beauty's apparent transcendence while acknowledging that perceived ends can generate teleological thought.
The earlier appeal to numinous beauty and aesthetic longing as experiential indications of divine reality.

O'Connor analyzes the strained expression associated with beauty, connects aesthetic attraction with negative emotion and artistic suffering, and traces it to a sense that reality falls short of an intended condition.
Aesthetic experience may point beyond itself and count as a candidate for experiencing God, especially where music's emotional power is discovered rather than invented.
This is a significant skeptical concession that aesthetic experience has evidential potential for theism even though O'Connor rejects treating it as a straightforward proof.
The earlier claim that beauty, music, and numinous experience can reveal a God seeking relationship with human beings.

O'Connor says analysis can obstruct aesthetic experience, declines a crude deductive argument, yet grants that beauty can seem outward-pointing and that music's affective capacity was found rather than humanly created.
Evolved neural and social functions of music do not diminish its divine significance because human brains can be intended instruments of revelation.
It directly rebuts a reductionistic explanation of beauty by arguing that evolutionary mechanisms and divine purpose are compatible rather than mutually exclusive.
O'Connor's suggestion that aesthetic faculties appear evolutionarily unnecessary or may admit a reductionistic natural explanation.

Collins describes specialized musical processing and the communal functions of song, concedes possible evolutionary explanations, and argues that such explanations leave room for God to use the brain for revelation.
A reductionistic evolutionary account of aesthetic preferences is available, but invoking it does not remove beauty's status as a genuine mystery.
The move states the skeptical alternative to the argument from beauty while preserving epistemic modesty about what that alternative ultimately explains.
Collins's claim that evolved aesthetic capacities can retain theological significance and serve as means of revelation.

O'Connor sketches how perceptual capacities might be co-opted into artificially stimulating art and music, but declines to press the reduction and agrees that the phenomenon remains deeply mysterious.
Fine-tuning, suffering, beauty, and the resurrection remain profound mysteries that do not justify confident conclusions about God's existence.
This is the closing synthesis of skeptical agnosticism across nearly every evidential domain named in the motion and explains why none warrants confidence.
The preceding theistic and skeptical arguments that assign evidential force to fine-tuning, suffering, beauty, and resurrection.
O'Connor treats the disputed phenomena as impressive or terrible mysteries, contrasts them with claims of certainty, and says confident answers to consequential questions about God deserve suspicion.
Whether God exists is life's most important question because ignoring a caring God and worshiping a nonexistent one are both seriously consequential errors.
The move explains the existential stakes of the entire motion and grounds Collins's sustained inquiry in both practical consequences and personal experience.

Collins presents symmetrical costs of getting the God question wrong, recalls being challenged by a suffering patient to examine his beliefs, and describes both participants as continuing along an uncertain road.
The God question merits exploration because it opens many fields of inquiry and even a small possibility of divine truth carries extraordinary significance.
The final substantive move states why a skeptical agnostic should still investigate the motion, combining intellectual breadth with a possibility-based account of its stakes.
Collins's preceding position that God's existence is the most important question and that both speakers remain on a continuing road of inquiry.

O'Connor emphasizes that discussion of God spans physics, beauty, history, ethics, and scripture; he argues Christianity would be maximally important if true and still worth examining under uncertainty.
